1: # Anthropic Python API library
2: 
3: <!-- prettier-ignore -->
4: [![PyPI version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/anthropic.svg?label=pypi%20(stable))](https://pypi.org/project/anthropic/)
5: 
6: The Anthropic Python library provides convenient access to the Anthropic REST API from any Python 3.8+
7: application. It includes type definitions for all request params and response fields,
8: and offers both synchronous and asynchronous clients powered by [httpx](https://github.com/encode/httpx).
9: 
10: ## Documentation
11: 
12: The REST API documentation can be found on [docs.anthropic.com](https://docs.anthropic.com/claude/reference/). The full API of this library can be found in [api.md](api.md).
13: 
14: ## Installation
15: 
16: ```sh
17: # install from PyPI
18: pip install anthropic
19: ```
20: 
21: ## Usage
22: 
23: The full API of this library can be found in [api.md](api.md).
24: 
25: ```python
26: import os
27: from anthropic import Anthropic
28: 
29: client = Anthropic(
30:     api_key=os.environ.get("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"),  # This is the default and can be omitted
31: )
32: 
33: message = client.messages.create(
34:     max_tokens=1024,
35:     messages=[
36:         {
37:             "role": "user",
38:             "content": "Hello, Claude",
39:         }
40:     ],
41:     model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
42: )
43: print(message.content)
44: ```
45: 
46: While you can provide an `api_key` keyword argument,
47: we recommend using [python-dotenv](https://pypi.org/project/python-dotenv/)
48: to add `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="my-anthropic-api-key"` to your `.env` file
49: so that your API Key is not stored in source control.
50: 
51: ## Async usage
52: 
53: Simply import `AsyncAnthropic` instead of `Anthropic` and use `await` with each API call:
54: 
55: ```python
56: import os
57: import asyncio
58: from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic
59: 
60: client = AsyncAnthropic(
61:     api_key=os.environ.get("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"),  # This is the default and can be omitted
62: )
63: 
64: 
65: async def main() -> None:
66:     message = await client.messages.create(
67:         max_tokens=1024,
68:         messages=[
69:             {
70:                 "role": "user",
71:                 "content": "Hello, Claude",
72:             }
73:         ],
74:         model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
75:     )
76:     print(message.content)
77: 
78: 
79: asyncio.run(main())
80: ```
81: 
82: Functionality between the synchronous and asynchronous clients is otherwise identical.
83: 
84: ### With aiohttp
85: 
86: By default, the async client uses `httpx` for HTTP requests. However, for improved concurrency performance you may also use `aiohttp` as the HTTP backend.
87: 
88: You can enable this by installing `aiohttp`:
89: 
90: ```sh
91: # install from PyPI
92: pip install anthropic[aiohttp]
93: ```
94: 
95: Then you can enable it by instantiating the client with `http_client=DefaultAioHttpClient()`:
96: 
97: ```python
98: import asyncio
99: from anthropic import DefaultAioHttpClient
100: from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic
101: 
102: 
103: async def main() -> None:
104:     async with AsyncAnthropic(
105:         api_key="my-anthropic-api-key",
106:         http_client=DefaultAioHttpClient(),
107:     ) as client:
108:         message = await client.messages.create(
109:             max_tokens=1024,
110:             messages=[
111:                 {
112:                     "role": "user",
113:                     "content": "Hello, Claude",
114:                 }
115:             ],
116:             model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
117:         )
118:         print(message.content)
119: 
120: 
121: asyncio.run(main())
122: ```
123: 
124: ## Streaming responses
125: 
126: We provide support for streaming responses using Server Side Events (SSE).
127: 
128: ```python
129: from anthropic import Anthropic
130: 
131: client = Anthropic()
132: 
133: stream = client.messages.create(
134:     max_tokens=1024,
135:     messages=[
136:         {
137:             "role": "user",
138:             "content": "Hello, Claude",
139:         }
140:     ],
141:     model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
142:     stream=True,
143: )
144: for event in stream:
145:     print(event.type)
146: ```
147: 
148: The async client uses the exact same interface.
149: 
150: ```python
151: from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic
152: 
153: client = AsyncAnthropic()
154: 
155: stream = await client.messages.create(
156:     max_tokens=1024,
157:     messages=[
158:         {
159:             "role": "user",
160:             "content": "Hello, Claude",
161:         }
162:     ],
163:     model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
164:     stream=True,
165: )
166: async for event in stream:
167:     print(event.type)
168: ```
169: 
170: ### Tool helpers
171: 
172: This library provides helper functions for defining and running tools as pure python functions, for example:
173: 
174: ```py
175: import json
176: import rich
177: from typing_extensions import Literal
178: from anthropic import Anthropic, beta_tool
179: 
180: client = Anthropic()
181: 
182: 
183: @beta_tool
184: def get_weather(location: str) -> str:
185:     """Lookup the weather for a given city in either celsius or fahrenheit
186: 
187:     Args:
188:         location: The city and state, e.g. San Francisco, CA
189:     Returns:
190:         A dictionary containing the location, temperature, and weather condition.
191:     """
192:     # Here you would typically make an API call to a weather service
193:     # For demonstration, we return a mock response
194:     return json.dumps(
195:         {
196:             "location": location,
197:             "temperature": "68°F",
198:             "condition": "Sunny",
199:         }
200:     )
201: 
202: 
203: runner = client.beta.messages.tool_runner(
204:     max_tokens=1024,
205:     model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
206:     tools=[get_weather],
207:     messages=[
208:         {"role": "user", "content": "What is the weather in SF?"},
209:     ],
210: )
211: for message in runner:
212:     rich.print(message)
213: ```
214: 
215: On every iteration, an API request will be made, if Claude wants to call one of the given tools then it will be automatically called, and the result will be returned directly to the model in the next iteration.
216: 
217: For more information see the [full docs](tools.md).
218: 
219: ### Streaming Helpers
220: 
221: This library provides several conveniences for streaming messages, for example:
222: 
223: ```py
224: import asyncio
225: from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic
226: 
227: client = AsyncAnthropic()
228: 
229: async def main() -> None:
230:     async with client.messages.stream(
231:         max_tokens=1024,
232:         messages=[
233:             {
234:                 "role": "user",
235:                 "content": "Say hello there!",
236:             }
237:         ],
238:         model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
239:     ) as stream:
240:         async for text in stream.text_stream:
241:             print(text, end="", flush=True)
242:         print()
243: 
244:     message = await stream.get_final_message()
245:     print(message.to_json())
246: 
247: asyncio.run(main())
248: ```
249: 
250: Streaming with `client.messages.stream(...)` exposes [various helpers for your convenience](helpers.md) including accumulation & SDK-specific events.
251: 
252: Alternatively, you can use `client.messages.create(..., stream=True)` which only returns an async iterable of the events in the stream and thus uses less memory (it does not build up a final message object for you).
253: 
254: ## Token counting
255: 
256: To get the token count for a message without creating it you can use the `client.messages.count_tokens()` method. This takes the same `messages` list as the `.create()` method.
257: 
258: ```py
259: count = client.messages.count_tokens(
260:     model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
261:     messages=[
262:         {"role": "user", "content": "Hello, world"}
263:     ]
264: )
265: count.input_tokens  # 10
266: ```
267: 
268: You can also see the exact usage for a given request through the `usage` response property, e.g.
269: 
270: ```py
271: message = client.messages.create(...)
272: message.usage
273: # Usage(input_tokens=25, output_tokens=13)
274: ```
275: 
276: ## Message Batches
277: 
278: This SDK provides support for the [Message Batches API](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/message-batches) under the `client.messages.batches` namespace.
279: 
280: ### Creating a batch
281: 
282: Message Batches take the exact same request params as the standard Messages API:
283: 
284: ```python
285: await client.messages.batches.create(
286:     requests=[
287:         {
288:             "custom_id": "my-first-request",
289:             "params": {
290:                 "model": "claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
291:                 "max_tokens": 1024,
292:                 "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello, world"}],
293:             },
294:         },
295:         {
296:             "custom_id": "my-second-request",
297:             "params": {
298:                 "model": "claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
299:                 "max_tokens": 1024,
300:                 "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hi again, friend"}],
301:             },
302:         },
303:     ]
304: )
305: ```
306: 
307: ### Getting results from a batch
308: 
309: Once a Message Batch has been processed, indicated by `.processing_status === 'ended'`, you can access the results with `.batches.results()`
310: 
311: ```python
312: result_stream = await client.messages.batches.results(batch_id)
313: async for entry in result_stream:
314:     if entry.result.type == "succeeded":
315:         print(entry.result.message.content)
316: ```
317: 
318: ## Tool use
319: 
320: This SDK provides support for tool use, aka function calling. More details can be found in [the documentation](https://docs.anthropic.com/claude/docs/tool-use).
321: 
322: ## AWS Bedrock
323: 
324: This library also provides support for the [Anthropic Bedrock API](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/claude/) if you install this library with the `bedrock` extra, e.g. `pip install -U anthropic[bedrock]`.
325: 
326: You can then import and instantiate a separate `AnthropicBedrock` class, the rest of the API is the same.
327: 
328: ```py
329: from anthropic import AnthropicBedrock
330: 
331: client = AnthropicBedrock()
332: 
333: message = client.messages.create(
334:     max_tokens=1024,
335:     messages=[
336:         {
337:             "role": "user",
338:             "content": "Hello!",
339:         }
340:     ],
341:     model="anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0",
342: )
343: print(message)
344: ```
345: 
346: The bedrock client supports the following arguments for authentication
347: 
348: ```py
349: AnthropicBedrock(
350:   aws_profile='...',
351:   aws_region='us-east'
352:   aws_secret_key='...',
353:   aws_access_key='...',
354:   aws_session_token='...',
355: )
356: ```
357: 
358: For a more fully fledged example see [`examples/bedrock.py`](https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python/blob/main/examples/bedrock.py).
359: 
360: ## Google Vertex
361: 
362: This library also provides support for the [Anthropic Vertex API](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai?hl=en) if you install this library with the `vertex` extra, e.g. `pip install -U anthropic[vertex]`.
363: 
364: You can then import and instantiate a separate `AnthropicVertex`/`AsyncAnthropicVertex` class, which has the same API as the base `Anthropic`/`AsyncAnthropic` class.
365: 
366: ```py
367: from anthropic import AnthropicVertex
368: 
369: client = AnthropicVertex()
370: 
371: message = client.messages.create(
372:     model="claude-sonnet-4@20250514",
373:     max_tokens=100,
374:     messages=[
375:         {
376:             "role": "user",
377:             "content": "Hello!",
378:         }
379:     ],
380: )
381: print(message)
382: ```
383: 
384: For a more complete example see [`examples/vertex.py`](https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python/blob/main/examples/vertex.py).
385: 
386: ## Using types
387: 
388: Nested request parameters are [TypedDicts](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.TypedDict). Responses are [Pydantic models](https://docs.pydantic.dev) which also provide helper methods for things like:
389: 
390: - Serializing back into JSON, `model.to_json()`
391: - Converting to a dictionary, `model.to_dict()`
392: 
393: Typed requests and responses provide autocomplete and documentation within your editor. If you would like to see type errors in VS Code to help catch bugs earlier, set `python.analysis.typeCheckingMode` to `basic`.
394: 
395: ## Pagination
396: 
397: List methods in the Anthropic API are paginated.
398: 
399: This library provides auto-paginating iterators with each list response, so you do not have to request successive pages manually:
400: 
401: ```python
402: from anthropic import Anthropic
403: 
404: client = Anthropic()
405: 
406: all_batches = []
407: # Automatically fetches more pages as needed.
408: for batch in client.messages.batches.list(
409:     limit=20,
410: ):
411:     # Do something with batch here
412:     all_batches.append(batch)
413: print(all_batches)
414: ```
415: 
416: Or, asynchronously:
417: 
418: ```python
419: import asyncio
420: from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic
421: 
422: client = AsyncAnthropic()
423: 
424: 
425: async def main() -> None:
426:     all_batches = []
427:     # Iterate through items across all pages, issuing requests as needed.
428:     async for batch in client.messages.batches.list(
429:         limit=20,
430:     ):
431:         all_batches.append(batch)
432:     print(all_batches)
433: 
434: 
435: asyncio.run(main())
436: ```
437: 
438: Alternatively, you can use the `.has_next_page()`, `.next_page_info()`, or `.get_next_page()` methods for more granular control working with pages:
439: 
440: ```python
441: first_page = await client.messages.batches.list(
442:     limit=20,
443: )
444: if first_page.has_next_page():
445:     print(f"will fetch next page using these details: {first_page.next_page_info()}")
446:     next_page = await first_page.get_next_page()
447:     print(f"number of items we just fetched: {len(next_page.data)}")
448: 
449: # Remove `await` for non-async usage.
450: ```
451: 
452: Or just work directly with the returned data:
453: 
454: ```python
455: first_page = await client.messages.batches.list(
456:     limit=20,
457: )
458: 
459: print(f"next page cursor: {first_page.last_id}")  # => "next page cursor: ..."
460: for batch in first_page.data:
461:     print(batch.id)
462: 
463: # Remove `await` for non-async usage.
464: ```
465: 
466: ## Nested params
467: 
468: Nested parameters are dictionaries, typed using `TypedDict`, for example:
469: 
470: ```python
471: from anthropic import Anthropic
472: 
473: client = Anthropic()
474: 
475: message = client.messages.create(
476:     max_tokens=1024,
477:     messages=[
478:         {
479:             "content": "Hello, world",
480:             "role": "user",
481:         }
482:     ],
483:     model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
484:     metadata={},
485: )
486: print(message.metadata)
487: ```
488: 
489: ## File uploads
490: 
491: Request parameters that correspond to file uploads can be passed as `bytes`, or a [`PathLike`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.PathLike) instance or a tuple of `(filename, contents, media type)`.
492: 
493: ```python
494: from pathlib import Path
495: from anthropic import Anthropic
496: 
497: client = Anthropic()
498: 
499: client.beta.files.upload(
500:     file=Path("/path/to/file"),
501: )
502: ```
503: 
504: The async client uses the exact same interface. If you pass a [`PathLike`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.PathLike) instance, the file contents will be read asynchronously automatically.
505: 
506: ## Handling errors
507: 
508: When the library is unable to connect to the API (for example, due to network connection problems or a timeout), a subclass of `anthropic.APIConnectionError` is raised.
509: 
510: When the API returns a non-success status code (that is, 4xx or 5xx
511: response), a subclass of `anthropic.APIStatusError` is raised, containing `status_code` and `response` properties.
512: 
513: All errors inherit from `anthropic.APIError`.
514: 
515: ```python
516: import anthropic
517: from anthropic import Anthropic
518: 
519: client = Anthropic()
520: 
521: try:
522:     client.messages.create(
523:         max_tokens=1024,
524:         messages=[
525:             {
526:                 "role": "user",
527:                 "content": "Hello, Claude",
528:             }
529:         ],
530:         model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
531:     )
532: except anthropic.APIConnectionError as e:
533:     print("The server could not be reached")
534:     print(e.__cause__)  # an underlying Exception, likely raised within httpx.
535: except anthropic.RateLimitError as e:
536:     print("A 429 status code was received; we should back off a bit.")
537: except anthropic.APIStatusError as e:
538:     print("Another non-200-range status code was received")
539:     print(e.status_code)
540:     print(e.response)
541: ```
542: 
543: Error codes are as follows:
544: 
545: | Status Code | Error Type                 |
546: | ----------- | -------------------------- |
547: | 400         | `BadRequestError`          |
548: | 401         | `AuthenticationError`      |
549: | 403         | `PermissionDeniedError`    |
550: | 404         | `NotFoundError`            |
551: | 422         | `UnprocessableEntityError` |
552: | 429         | `RateLimitError`           |
553: | >=500       | `InternalServerError`      |
554: | N/A         | `APIConnectionError`       |
555: 
556: ## Request IDs
557: 
558: > For more information on debugging requests, see [these docs](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/api/errors#request-id)
559: 
560: All object responses in the SDK provide a `_request_id` property which is added from the `request-id` response header so that you can quickly log failing requests and report them back to Anthropic.
561: 
562: ```python
563: message = client.messages.create(
564:     max_tokens=1024,
565:     messages=[
566:         {
567:             "role": "user",
568:             "content": "Hello, Claude",
569:         }
570:     ],
571:     model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
572: )
573: print(message._request_id)  # req_018EeWyXxfu5pfWkrYcMdjWG
574: ```
575: 
576: Note that unlike other properties that use an `_` prefix, the `_request_id` property
577: _is_ public. Unless documented otherwise, _all_ other `_` prefix properties,
578: methods and modules are _private_.
579: 
580: ### Retries
581: 
582: Certain errors are automatically retried 2 times by default, with a short exponential backoff.
583: Connection errors (for example, due to a network connectivity problem), 408 Request Timeout, 409 Conflict,
584: 429 Rate Limit, and >=500 Internal errors are all retried by default.
585: 
586: You can use the `max_retries` option to configure or disable retry settings:
587: 
588: ```python
589: from anthropic import Anthropic
590: 
591: # Configure the default for all requests:
592: client = Anthropic(
593:     # default is 2
594:     max_retries=0,
595: )
596: 
597: # Or, configure per-request:
598: client.with_options(max_retries=5).messages.create(
599:     max_tokens=1024,
600:     messages=[
601:         {
602:             "role": "user",
603:             "content": "Hello, Claude",
604:         }
605:     ],
606:     model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
607: )
608: ```
609: 
610: ### Timeouts
611: 
612: By default requests time out after 10 minutes. You can configure this with a `timeout` option,
613: which accepts a float or an [`httpx.Timeout`](https://www.python-httpx.org/advanced/timeouts/#fine-tuning-the-configuration) object:
614: 
615: ```python
616: from anthropic import Anthropic
617: 
618: # Configure the default for all requests:
619: client = Anthropic(
620:     # 20 seconds (default is 10 minutes)
621:     timeout=20.0,
622: )
623: 
624: # More granular control:
625: client = Anthropic(
626:     timeout=httpx.Timeout(60.0, read=5.0, write=10.0, connect=2.0),
627: )
628: 
629: # Override per-request:
630: client.with_options(timeout=5.0).messages.create(
631:     max_tokens=1024,
632:     messages=[
633:         {
634:             "role": "user",
635:             "content": "Hello, Claude",
636:         }
637:     ],
638:     model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
639: )
640: ```
641: 
642: On timeout, an `APITimeoutError` is thrown.
643: 
644: Note that requests that time out are [retried twice by default](#retries).
645: 
646: ### Long Requests
647: 
648: > [!IMPORTANT]
649: > We highly encourage you use the streaming [Messages API](#streaming-responses) for longer running requests.
650: 
651: We do not recommend setting a large `max_tokens` values without using streaming.
652: Some networks may drop idle connections after a certain period of time, which
653: can cause the request to fail or [timeout](#timeouts) without receiving a response from Anthropic.
654: 
655: This SDK will also throw a `ValueError` if a non-streaming request is expected to be above roughly 10 minutes long.
656: Passing `stream=True` or [overriding](#timeouts) the `timeout` option at the client or request level disables this error.
657: 
658: An expected request latency longer than the [timeout](#timeouts) for a non-streaming request
659: will result in the client terminating the connection and retrying without receiving a response.
660: 
661: We set a [TCP socket keep-alive](https://tldp.org/HOWTO/TCP-Keepalive-HOWTO/overview.html) option in order
662: to reduce the impact of idle connection timeouts on some networks.
663: This can be [overriden](#Configuring-the-HTTP-client) by passing a `http_client` option to the client.
664: 
665: ## Default Headers
666: 
667: We automatically send the `anthropic-version` header set to `2023-06-01`.
668: 
669: If you need to, you can override it by setting default headers per-request or on the client object.
670: 
671: Be aware that doing so may result in incorrect types and other unexpected or undefined behavior in the SDK.
672: 
673: ```python
674: from anthropic import Anthropic
675: 
676: client = Anthropic(
677:     default_headers={"anthropic-version": "My-Custom-Value"},
678: )
679: ```
680: 
681: ## Advanced
682: 
683: ### Logging
684: 
685: We use the standard library [`logging`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html) module.
686: 
687: You can enable logging by setting the environment variable `ANTHROPIC_LOG` to `info`.
688: 
689: ```shell
690: $ export ANTHROPIC_LOG=info
691: ```
692: 
693: Or to `debug` for more verbose logging.
694: 
695: ### How to tell whether `None` means `null` or missing
696: 
697: In an API response, a field may be explicitly `null`, or missing entirely; in either case, its value is `None` in this library. You can differentiate the two cases with `.model_fields_set`:
698: 
699: ```py
700: if response.my_field is None:
701:   if 'my_field' not in response.model_fields_set:
702:     print('Got json like {}, without a "my_field" key present at all.')
703:   else:
704:     print('Got json like {"my_field": null}.')
705: ```
706: 
707: ### Accessing raw response data (e.g. headers)
708: 
709: The "raw" Response object can be accessed by prefixing `.with_raw_response.` to any HTTP method call, e.g.,
710: 
711: ```py
712: from anthropic import Anthropic
713: 
714: client = Anthropic()
715: response = client.messages.with_raw_response.create(
716:     max_tokens=1024,
717:     messages=[{
718:         "role": "user",
719:         "content": "Hello, Claude",
720:     }],
721:     model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
722: )
723: print(response.headers.get('X-My-Header'))
724: 
725: message = response.parse()  # get the object that `messages.create()` would have returned
726: print(message.content)
727: ```
728: 
729: These methods return a [`LegacyAPIResponse`](https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python/tree/main/src/anthropic/_legacy_response.py) object. This is a legacy class as we're changing it slightly in the next major version.
730: 
731: For the sync client this will mostly be the same with the exception
732: of `content` & `text` will be methods instead of properties. In the
733: async client, all methods will be async.
734: 
735: A migration script will be provided & the migration in general should
736: be smooth.
737: 
738: #### `.with_streaming_response`
739: 
740: The above interface eagerly reads the full response body when you make the request, which may not always be what you want.
741: 
742: To stream the response body, use `.with_streaming_response` instead, which requires a context manager and only reads the response body once you call `.read()`, `.text()`, `.json()`, `.iter_bytes()`, `.iter_text()`, `.iter_lines()` or `.parse()`. In the async client, these are async methods.
743: 
744: As such, `.with_streaming_response` methods return a different [`APIResponse`](https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python/tree/main/src/anthropic/_response.py) object, and the async client returns an [`AsyncAPIResponse`](https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python/tree/main/src/anthropic/_response.py) object.
745: 
746: ```python
747: with client.messages.with_streaming_response.create(
748:     max_tokens=1024,
749:     messages=[
750:         {
751:             "role": "user",
752:             "content": "Hello, Claude",
753:         }
754:     ],
755:     model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
756: ) as response:
757:     print(response.headers.get("X-My-Header"))
758: 
759:     for line in response.iter_lines():
760:         print(line)
761: ```
762: 
763: The context manager is required so that the response will reliably be closed.
764: 
765: ### Making custom/undocumented requests
766: 
767: This library is typed for convenient access to the documented API.
768: 
769: If you need to access undocumented endpoints, params, or response properties, the library can still be used.
770: 
771: #### Undocumented endpoints
772: 
773: To make requests to undocumented endpoints, you can make requests using `client.get`, `client.post`, and other
774: http verbs. Options on the client will be respected (such as retries) when making this request.
775: 
776: ```py
777: import httpx
778: 
779: response = client.post(
780:     "/foo",
781:     cast_to=httpx.Response,
782:     body={"my_param": True},
783: )
784: 
785: print(response.headers.get("x-foo"))
786: ```
787: 
788: #### Undocumented request params
789: 
790: If you want to explicitly send an extra param, you can do so with the `extra_query`, `extra_body`, and `extra_headers` request
791: options.
792: 
793: > [!WARNING]
794: >
795: > The `extra_` parameters of the same name overrides the documented parameters. For security reasons, ensure these methods are only used with trusted input data.
796: 
797: #### Undocumented response properties
798: 
799: To access undocumented response properties, you can access the extra fields like `response.unknown_prop`. You
800: can also get all the extra fields on the Pydantic model as a dict with
801: [`response.model_extra`](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/api/base_model/#pydantic.BaseModel.model_extra).
802: 
803: ### Configuring the HTTP client
804: 
805: You can directly override the [httpx client](https://www.python-httpx.org/api/#client) to customize it for your use case, including:
806: 
807: - Support for [proxies](https://www.python-httpx.org/advanced/proxies/)
808: - Custom [transports](https://www.python-httpx.org/advanced/transports/)
809: - Additional [advanced](https://www.python-httpx.org/advanced/clients/) functionality
810: 
811: ```python
812: import httpx
813: from anthropic import Anthropic, DefaultHttpxClient
814: 
815: client = Anthropic(
816:     # Or use the `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` env var
817:     base_url="http://my.test.server.example.com:8083",
818:     http_client=DefaultHttpxClient(
819:         proxy="http://my.test.proxy.example.com",
820:         transport=httpx.HTTPTransport(local_address="0.0.0.0"),
821:     ),
822: )
823: ```
824: 
825: You can also customize the client on a per-request basis by using `with_options()`:
826: 
827: ```python
828: client.with_options(http_client=DefaultHttpxClient(...))
829: ```
830: 
831: ### Managing HTTP resources
832: 
833: By default the library closes underlying HTTP connections whenever the client is [garbage collected](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html#object.__del__). You can manually close the client using the `.close()` method if desired, or with a context manager that closes when exiting.
834: 
835: ```py
836: from anthropic import Anthropic
837: 
838: with Anthropic() as client:
839:   # make requests here
840:   ...
841: 
842: # HTTP client is now closed
843: ```
844: 
845: ## Versioning
846: 
847: This package generally follows [SemVer](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html) conventions, though certain backwards-incompatible changes may be released as minor versions:
848: 
849: 1. Changes that only affect static types, without breaking runtime behavior.
850: 2. Changes to library internals which are technically public but not intended or documented for external use. _(Please open a GitHub issue to let us know if you are relying on such internals.)_
851: 3. Changes that we do not expect to impact the vast majority of users in practice.
852: 
853: We take backwards-compatibility seriously and work hard to ensure you can rely on a smooth upgrade experience.
854: 
855: We are keen for your feedback; please open an [issue](https://www.github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python/issues) with questions, bugs, or suggestions.
856: 
857: ### Determining the installed version
858: 
859: If you've upgraded to the latest version but aren't seeing any new features you were expecting then your python environment is likely still using an older version.
860: 
861: You can determine the version that is being used at runtime with:
862: 
863: ```py
864: import anthropic
865: print(anthropic.__version__)
866: ```
867: 
868: ## Requirements
869: 
870: Python 3.8 or higher.
871: 
872: ## Contributing
873: 
874: See [the contributing documentation](./CONTRIBUTING.md).

# Anthropic Python API library

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
[![PyPI version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/anthropic.svg?label=pypi%20(stable))](https://pypi.org/project/anthropic/)

The Anthropic Python library provides convenient access to the Anthropic REST API from any Python 3.8+
application. It includes type definitions for all request params and response fields,
and offers both synchronous and asynchronous clients powered by [httpx](https://github.com/encode/httpx).

## Documentation

The REST API documentation can be found on [docs.anthropic.com](https://docs.anthropic.com/claude/reference/). The full API of this library can be found in [api.md](api.md).

## Installation

```sh
# install from PyPI
pip install anthropic
```

## Usage

The full API of this library can be found in [api.md](api.md).

```python
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic(
    api_key=os.environ.get("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"),  # This is the default and can be omitted
)

message = client.messages.create(
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Hello, Claude",
        }
    ],
    model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
)
print(message.content)
```

While you can provide an `api_key` keyword argument,
we recommend using [python-dotenv](https://pypi.org/project/python-dotenv/)
to add `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="my-anthropic-api-key"` to your `.env` file
so that your API Key is not stored in source control.

## Async usage

Simply import `AsyncAnthropic` instead of `Anthropic` and use `await` with each API call:

```python
import os
import asyncio
from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic

client = AsyncAnthropic(
    api_key=os.environ.get("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"),  # This is the default and can be omitted
)


async def main() -> None:
    message = await client.messages.create(
        max_tokens=1024,
        messages=[
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": "Hello, Claude",
            }
        ],
        model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
    )
    print(message.content)


asyncio.run(main())
```

Functionality between the synchronous and asynchronous clients is otherwise identical.

### With aiohttp

By default, the async client uses `httpx` for HTTP requests. However, for improved concurrency performance you may also use `aiohttp` as the HTTP backend.

You can enable this by installing `aiohttp`:

```sh
# install from PyPI
pip install anthropic[aiohttp]
```

Then you can enable it by instantiating the client with `http_client=DefaultAioHttpClient()`:

```python
import asyncio
from anthropic import DefaultAioHttpClient
from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic


async def main() -> None:
    async with AsyncAnthropic(
        api_key="my-anthropic-api-key",
        http_client=DefaultAioHttpClient(),
    ) as client:
        message = await client.messages.create(
            max_tokens=1024,
            messages=[
                {
                    "role": "user",
                    "content": "Hello, Claude",
                }
            ],
            model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
        )
        print(message.content)


asyncio.run(main())
```

## Streaming responses

We provide support for streaming responses using Server Side Events (SSE).

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()

stream = client.messages.create(
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Hello, Claude",
        }
    ],
    model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
    stream=True,
)
for event in stream:
    print(event.type)
```

The async client uses the exact same interface.

```python
from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic

client = AsyncAnthropic()

stream = await client.messages.create(
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Hello, Claude",
        }
    ],
    model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
    stream=True,
)
async for event in stream:
    print(event.type)
```

### Tool helpers

This library provides helper functions for defining and running tools as pure python functions, for example:

```py
import json
import rich
from typing_extensions import Literal
from anthropic import Anthropic, beta_tool

client = Anthropic()


@beta_tool
def get_weather(location: str) -> str:
    """Lookup the weather for a given city in either celsius or fahrenheit

    Args:
        location: The city and state, e.g. San Francisco, CA
    Returns:
        A dictionary containing the location, temperature, and weather condition.
    """
    # Here you would typically make an API call to a weather service
    # For demonstration, we return a mock response
    return json.dumps(
        {
            "location": location,
            "temperature": "68°F",
            "condition": "Sunny",
        }
    )


runner = client.beta.messages.tool_runner(
    max_tokens=1024,
    model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
    tools=[get_weather],
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "What is the weather in SF?"},
    ],
)
for message in runner:
    rich.print(message)
```

On every iteration, an API request will be made, if Claude wants to call one of the given tools then it will be automatically called, and the result will be returned directly to the model in the next iteration.

For more information see the [full docs](tools.md).

### Streaming Helpers

This library provides several conveniences for streaming messages, for example:

```py
import asyncio
from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic

client = AsyncAnthropic()

async def main() -> None:
    async with client.messages.stream(
        max_tokens=1024,
        messages=[
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": "Say hello there!",
            }
        ],
        model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
    ) as stream:
        async for text in stream.text_stream:
            print(text, end="", flush=True)
        print()

    message = await stream.get_final_message()
    print(message.to_json())

asyncio.run(main())
```

Streaming with `client.messages.stream(...)` exposes [various helpers for your convenience](helpers.md) including accumulation & SDK-specific events.

Alternatively, you can use `client.messages.create(..., stream=True)` which only returns an async iterable of the events in the stream and thus uses less memory (it does not build up a final message object for you).

## Token counting

To get the token count for a message without creating it you can use the `client.messages.count_tokens()` method. This takes the same `messages` list as the `.create()` method.

```py
count = client.messages.count_tokens(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "Hello, world"}
    ]
)
count.input_tokens  # 10
```

You can also see the exact usage for a given request through the `usage` response property, e.g.

```py
message = client.messages.create(...)
message.usage
# Usage(input_tokens=25, output_tokens=13)
```

## Message Batches

This SDK provides support for the [Message Batches API](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/message-batches) under the `client.messages.batches` namespace.

### Creating a batch

Message Batches take the exact same request params as the standard Messages API:

```python
await client.messages.batches.create(
    requests=[
        {
            "custom_id": "my-first-request",
            "params": {
                "model": "claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
                "max_tokens": 1024,
                "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello, world"}],
            },
        },
        {
            "custom_id": "my-second-request",
            "params": {
                "model": "claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
                "max_tokens": 1024,
                "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hi again, friend"}],
            },
        },
    ]
)
```

### Getting results from a batch

Once a Message Batch has been processed, indicated by `.processing_status === 'ended'`, you can access the results with `.batches.results()`

```python
result_stream = await client.messages.batches.results(batch_id)
async for entry in result_stream:
    if entry.result.type == "succeeded":
        print(entry.result.message.content)
```

## Tool use

This SDK provides support for tool use, aka function calling. More details can be found in [the documentation](https://docs.anthropic.com/claude/docs/tool-use).

## AWS Bedrock

This library also provides support for the [Anthropic Bedrock API](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/claude/) if you install this library with the `bedrock` extra, e.g. `pip install -U anthropic[bedrock]`.

You can then import and instantiate a separate `AnthropicBedrock` class, the rest of the API is the same.

```py
from anthropic import AnthropicBedrock

client = AnthropicBedrock()

message = client.messages.create(
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Hello!",
        }
    ],
    model="anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0",
)
print(message)
```

The bedrock client supports the following arguments for authentication

```py
AnthropicBedrock(
  aws_profile='...',
  aws_region='us-east'
  aws_secret_key='...',
  aws_access_key='...',
  aws_session_token='...',
)
```

For a more fully fledged example see [`examples/bedrock.py`](https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python/blob/main/examples/bedrock.py).

## Google Vertex

This library also provides support for the [Anthropic Vertex API](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai?hl=en) if you install this library with the `vertex` extra, e.g. `pip install -U anthropic[vertex]`.

You can then import and instantiate a separate `AnthropicVertex`/`AsyncAnthropicVertex` class, which has the same API as the base `Anthropic`/`AsyncAnthropic` class.

```py
from anthropic import AnthropicVertex

client = AnthropicVertex()

message = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4@20250514",
    max_tokens=100,
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Hello!",
        }
    ],
)
print(message)
```

For a more complete example see [`examples/vertex.py`](https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python/blob/main/examples/vertex.py).

## Using types

Nested request parameters are [TypedDicts](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.TypedDict). Responses are [Pydantic models](https://docs.pydantic.dev) which also provide helper methods for things like:

- Serializing back into JSON, `model.to_json()`
- Converting to a dictionary, `model.to_dict()`

Typed requests and responses provide autocomplete and documentation within your editor. If you would like to see type errors in VS Code to help catch bugs earlier, set `python.analysis.typeCheckingMode` to `basic`.

## Pagination

List methods in the Anthropic API are paginated.

This library provides auto-paginating iterators with each list response, so you do not have to request successive pages manually:

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()

all_batches = []
# Automatically fetches more pages as needed.
for batch in client.messages.batches.list(
    limit=20,
):
    # Do something with batch here
    all_batches.append(batch)
print(all_batches)
```

Or, asynchronously:

```python
import asyncio
from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic

client = AsyncAnthropic()


async def main() -> None:
    all_batches = []
    # Iterate through items across all pages, issuing requests as needed.
    async for batch in client.messages.batches.list(
        limit=20,
    ):
        all_batches.append(batch)
    print(all_batches)


asyncio.run(main())
```

Alternatively, you can use the `.has_next_page()`, `.next_page_info()`, or `.get_next_page()` methods for more granular control working with pages:

```python
first_page = await client.messages.batches.list(
    limit=20,
)
if first_page.has_next_page():
    print(f"will fetch next page using these details: {first_page.next_page_info()}")
    next_page = await first_page.get_next_page()
    print(f"number of items we just fetched: {len(next_page.data)}")

# Remove `await` for non-async usage.
```

Or just work directly with the returned data:

```python
first_page = await client.messages.batches.list(
    limit=20,
)

print(f"next page cursor: {first_page.last_id}")  # => "next page cursor: ..."
for batch in first_page.data:
    print(batch.id)

# Remove `await` for non-async usage.
```

## Nested params

Nested parameters are dictionaries, typed using `TypedDict`, for example:

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()

message = client.messages.create(
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {
            "content": "Hello, world",
            "role": "user",
        }
    ],
    model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
    metadata={},
)
print(message.metadata)
```

## File uploads

Request parameters that correspond to file uploads can be passed as `bytes`, or a [`PathLike`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.PathLike) instance or a tuple of `(filename, contents, media type)`.

```python
from pathlib import Path
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()

client.beta.files.upload(
    file=Path("/path/to/file"),
)
```

The async client uses the exact same interface. If you pass a [`PathLike`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.PathLike) instance, the file contents will be read asynchronously automatically.

## Handling errors

When the library is unable to connect to the API (for example, due to network connection problems or a timeout), a subclass of `anthropic.APIConnectionError` is raised.

When the API returns a non-success status code (that is, 4xx or 5xx
response), a subclass of `anthropic.APIStatusError` is raised, containing `status_code` and `response` properties.

All errors inherit from `anthropic.APIError`.

```python
import anthropic
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()

try:
    client.messages.create(
        max_tokens=1024,
        messages=[
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": "Hello, Claude",
            }
        ],
        model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
    )
except anthropic.APIConnectionError as e:
    print("The server could not be reached")
    print(e.__cause__)  # an underlying Exception, likely raised within httpx.
except anthropic.RateLimitError as e:
    print("A 429 status code was received; we should back off a bit.")
except anthropic.APIStatusError as e:
    print("Another non-200-range status code was received")
    print(e.status_code)
    print(e.response)
```

Error codes are as follows:

| Status Code | Error Type                 |
| ----------- | -------------------------- |
| 400         | `BadRequestError`          |
| 401         | `AuthenticationError`      |
| 403         | `PermissionDeniedError`    |
| 404         | `NotFoundError`            |
| 422         | `UnprocessableEntityError` |
| 429         | `RateLimitError`           |
| >=500       | `InternalServerError`      |
| N/A         | `APIConnectionError`       |

## Request IDs

> For more information on debugging requests, see [these docs](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/api/errors#request-id)

All object responses in the SDK provide a `_request_id` property which is added from the `request-id` response header so that you can quickly log failing requests and report them back to Anthropic.

```python
message = client.messages.create(
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Hello, Claude",
        }
    ],
    model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
)
print(message._request_id)  # req_018EeWyXxfu5pfWkrYcMdjWG
```

Note that unlike other properties that use an `_` prefix, the `_request_id` property
_is_ public. Unless documented otherwise, _all_ other `_` prefix properties,
methods and modules are _private_.

### Retries

Certain errors are automatically retried 2 times by default, with a short exponential backoff.
Connection errors (for example, due to a network connectivity problem), 408 Request Timeout, 409 Conflict,
429 Rate Limit, and >=500 Internal errors are all retried by default.

You can use the `max_retries` option to configure or disable retry settings:

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

# Configure the default for all requests:
client = Anthropic(
    # default is 2
    max_retries=0,
)

# Or, configure per-request:
client.with_options(max_retries=5).messages.create(
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Hello, Claude",
        }
    ],
    model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
)
```

### Timeouts

By default requests time out after 10 minutes. You can configure this with a `timeout` option,
which accepts a float or an [`httpx.Timeout`](https://www.python-httpx.org/advanced/timeouts/#fine-tuning-the-configuration) object:

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

# Configure the default for all requests:
client = Anthropic(
    # 20 seconds (default is 10 minutes)
    timeout=20.0,
)

# More granular control:
client = Anthropic(
    timeout=httpx.Timeout(60.0, read=5.0, write=10.0, connect=2.0),
)

# Override per-request:
client.with_options(timeout=5.0).messages.create(
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Hello, Claude",
        }
    ],
    model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
)
```

On timeout, an `APITimeoutError` is thrown.

Note that requests that time out are [retried twice by default](#retries).

### Long Requests

> [!IMPORTANT]
> We highly encourage you use the streaming [Messages API](#streaming-responses) for longer running requests.

We do not recommend setting a large `max_tokens` values without using streaming.
Some networks may drop idle connections after a certain period of time, which
can cause the request to fail or [timeout](#timeouts) without receiving a response from Anthropic.

This SDK will also throw a `ValueError` if a non-streaming request is expected to be above roughly 10 minutes long.
Passing `stream=True` or [overriding](#timeouts) the `timeout` option at the client or request level disables this error.

An expected request latency longer than the [timeout](#timeouts) for a non-streaming request
will result in the client terminating the connection and retrying without receiving a response.

We set a [TCP socket keep-alive](https://tldp.org/HOWTO/TCP-Keepalive-HOWTO/overview.html) option in order
to reduce the impact of idle connection timeouts on some networks.
This can be [overriden](#Configuring-the-HTTP-client) by passing a `http_client` option to the client.

## Default Headers

We automatically send the `anthropic-version` header set to `2023-06-01`.

If you need to, you can override it by setting default headers per-request or on the client object.

Be aware that doing so may result in incorrect types and other unexpected or undefined behavior in the SDK.

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic(
    default_headers={"anthropic-version": "My-Custom-Value"},
)
```

## Advanced

### Logging

We use the standard library [`logging`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html) module.

You can enable logging by setting the environment variable `ANTHROPIC_LOG` to `info`.

```shell
$ export ANTHROPIC_LOG=info
```

Or to `debug` for more verbose logging.

### How to tell whether `None` means `null` or missing

In an API response, a field may be explicitly `null`, or missing entirely; in either case, its value is `None` in this library. You can differentiate the two cases with `.model_fields_set`:

```py
if response.my_field is None:
  if 'my_field' not in response.model_fields_set:
    print('Got json like {}, without a "my_field" key present at all.')
  else:
    print('Got json like {"my_field": null}.')
```

### Accessing raw response data (e.g. headers)

The "raw" Response object can be accessed by prefixing `.with_raw_response.` to any HTTP method call, e.g.,

```py
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()
response = client.messages.with_raw_response.create(
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{
        "role": "user",
        "content": "Hello, Claude",
    }],
    model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
)
print(response.headers.get('X-My-Header'))

message = response.parse()  # get the object that `messages.create()` would have returned
print(message.content)
```

These methods return a [`LegacyAPIResponse`](https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python/tree/main/src/anthropic/_legacy_response.py) object. This is a legacy class as we're changing it slightly in the next major version.

For the sync client this will mostly be the same with the exception
of `content` & `text` will be methods instead of properties. In the
async client, all methods will be async.

A migration script will be provided & the migration in general should
be smooth.

#### `.with_streaming_response`

The above interface eagerly reads the full response body when you make the request, which may not always be what you want.

To stream the response body, use `.with_streaming_response` instead, which requires a context manager and only reads the response body once you call `.read()`, `.text()`, `.json()`, `.iter_bytes()`, `.iter_text()`, `.iter_lines()` or `.parse()`. In the async client, these are async methods.

As such, `.with_streaming_response` methods return a different [`APIResponse`](https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python/tree/main/src/anthropic/_response.py) object, and the async client returns an [`AsyncAPIResponse`](https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python/tree/main/src/anthropic/_response.py) object.

```python
with client.messages.with_streaming_response.create(
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Hello, Claude",
        }
    ],
    model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",
) as response:
    print(response.headers.get("X-My-Header"))

    for line in response.iter_lines():
        print(line)
```

The context manager is required so that the response will reliably be closed.

### Making custom/undocumented requests

This library is typed for convenient access to the documented API.

If you need to access undocumented endpoints, params, or response properties, the library can still be used.

#### Undocumented endpoints

To make requests to undocumented endpoints, you can make requests using `client.get`, `client.post`, and other
http verbs. Options on the client will be respected (such as retries) when making this request.

```py
import httpx

response = client.post(
    "/foo",
    cast_to=httpx.Response,
    body={"my_param": True},
)

print(response.headers.get("x-foo"))
```

#### Undocumented request params

If you want to explicitly send an extra param, you can do so with the `extra_query`, `extra_body`, and `extra_headers` request
options.

> [!WARNING]
>
> The `extra_` parameters of the same name overrides the documented parameters. For security reasons, ensure these methods are only used with trusted input data.

#### Undocumented response properties

To access undocumented response properties, you can access the extra fields like `response.unknown_prop`. You
can also get all the extra fields on the Pydantic model as a dict with
[`response.model_extra`](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/api/base_model/#pydantic.BaseModel.model_extra).

### Configuring the HTTP client

You can directly override the [httpx client](https://www.python-httpx.org/api/#client) to customize it for your use case, including:

- Support for [proxies](https://www.python-httpx.org/advanced/proxies/)
- Custom [transports](https://www.python-httpx.org/advanced/transports/)
- Additional [advanced](https://www.python-httpx.org/advanced/clients/) functionality

```python
import httpx
from anthropic import Anthropic, DefaultHttpxClient

client = Anthropic(
    # Or use the `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` env var
    base_url="http://my.test.server.example.com:8083",
    http_client=DefaultHttpxClient(
        proxy="http://my.test.proxy.example.com",
        transport=httpx.HTTPTransport(local_address="0.0.0.0"),
    ),
)
```

You can also customize the client on a per-request basis by using `with_options()`:

```python
client.with_options(http_client=DefaultHttpxClient(...))
```

### Managing HTTP resources

By default the library closes underlying HTTP connections whenever the client is [garbage collected](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html#object.__del__). You can manually close the client using the `.close()` method if desired, or with a context manager that closes when exiting.

```py
from anthropic import Anthropic

with Anthropic() as client:
  # make requests here
  ...

# HTTP client is now closed
```

## Versioning

This package generally follows [SemVer](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html) conventions, though certain backwards-incompatible changes may be released as minor versions:

1. Changes that only affect static types, without breaking runtime behavior.
2. Changes to library internals which are technically public but not intended or documented for external use. _(Please open a GitHub issue to let us know if you are relying on such internals.)_
3. Changes that we do not expect to impact the vast majority of users in practice.

We take backwards-compatibility seriously and work hard to ensure you can rely on a smooth upgrade experience.

We are keen for your feedback; please open an [issue](https://www.github.com/anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python/issues) with questions, bugs, or suggestions.

### Determining the installed version

If you've upgraded to the latest version but aren't seeing any new features you were expecting then your python environment is likely still using an older version.

You can determine the version that is being used at runtime with:

```py
import anthropic
print(anthropic.__version__)
```

## Requirements

Python 3.8 or higher.

## Contributing

See [the contributing documentation](./CONTRIBUTING.md).

from typing import Any, cast
from functools import partial
from urllib.parse import unquote

import pytest

from anthropic._qs import Querystring, stringify


def test_empty() -> None:
    assert stringify({}) == ""
    assert stringify({"a": {}}) == ""
    assert stringify({"a": {"b": {"c": {}}}}) == ""


def test_basic() -> None:
    assert stringify({"a": 1}) == "a=1"
    assert stringify({"a": "b"}) == "a=b"
    assert stringify({"a": True}) == "a=true"
    assert stringify({"a": False}) == "a=false"
    assert stringify({"a": 1.23456}) == "a=1.23456"
    assert stringify({"a": None}) == ""


@pytest.mark.parametrize("method", ["class", "function"])
def test_nested_dotted(method: str) -> None:
    if method == "class":
        serialise = Querystring(nested_format="dots").stringify
    else:
        serialise = partial(stringify, nested_format="dots")

    assert unquote(serialise({"a": {"b": "c"}})) == "a.b=c"
    assert unquote(serialise({"a": {"b": "c", "d": "e", "f": "g"}})) == "a.b=c&a.d=e&a.f=g"
    assert unquote(serialise({"a": {"b": {"c": {"d": "e"}}}})) == "a.b.c.d=e"
    assert unquote(serialise({"a": {"b": True}})) == "a.b=true"


def test_nested_brackets() -> None:
    assert unquote(stringify({"a": {"b": "c"}})) == "a[b]=c"
    assert unquote(stringify({"a": {"b": "c", "d": "e", "f": "g"}})) == "a[b]=c&a[d]=e&a[f]=g"
    assert unquote(stringify({"a": {"b": {"c": {"d": "e"}}}})) == "a[b][c][d]=e"
    assert unquote(stringify({"a": {"b": True}})) == "a[b]=true"


@pytest.mark.parametrize("method", ["class", "function"])
def test_array_comma(method: str) -> None:
    if method == "class":
        serialise = Querystring(array_format="comma").stringify
    else:
        serialise = partial(stringify, array_format="comma")

    assert unquote(serialise({"in": ["foo", "bar"]})) == "in=foo,bar"
    assert unquote(serialise({"a": {"b": [True, False]}})) == "a[b]=true,false"
    assert unquote(serialise({"a": {"b": [True, False, None, True]}})) == "a[b]=true,false,true"


def test_array_repeat() -> None:
    assert unquote(stringify({"in": ["foo", "bar"]})) == "in=foo&in=bar"
    assert unquote(stringify({"a": {"b": [True, False]}})) == "a[b]=true&a[b]=false"
    assert unquote(stringify({"a": {"b": [True, False, None, True]}})) == "a[b]=true&a[b]=false&a[b]=true"
    assert unquote(stringify({"in": ["foo", {"b": {"c": ["d", "e"]}}]})) == "in=foo&in[b][c]=d&in[b][c]=e"


@pytest.mark.parametrize("method", ["class", "function"])
def test_array_brackets(method: str) -> None:
    if method == "class":
        serialise = Querystring(array_format="brackets").stringify
    else:
        serialise = partial(stringify, array_format="brackets")

    assert unquote(serialise({"in": ["foo", "bar"]})) == "in[]=foo&in[]=bar"
    assert unquote(serialise({"a": {"b": [True, False]}})) == "a[b][]=true&a[b][]=false"
    assert unquote(serialise({"a": {"b": [True, False, None, True]}})) == "a[b][]=true&a[b][]=false&a[b][]=true"


def test_unknown_array_format() -> None:
    with pytest.raises(NotImplementedError, match="Unknown array_format value: foo, choose from comma, repeat"):
        stringify({"a": ["foo", "bar"]}, array_format=cast(Any, "foo"))
